svg.aria-label: Diagram: how a GuardDuty declarative policy decides coverage per Region, and the three ways a Region ends up with no protection. The policy document nests a guardduty key, an enablement key, and then one or more blocks: an optional default block applying to every Region where GuardDuty is available, and optional Region-specific blocks keyed by Region name. A policy must contain at least one block. The resolution rule is that a Region-specific block fully replaces the default for that Region and is not merged with it, so any feature omitted from a Region block is not inherited from the default. A Region with neither a default block nor a Region-specific block is unmanaged: the policy neither enables nor disables GuardDuty there and existing settings are left unchanged. Within any block, foundational threat detection must be enabled if any other feature in that same block is enabled. Three failure paths are drawn. First, a Region override written to disable one feature, which silently drops every other feature the default had enabled in that Region unless all of them are re-listed; AWS's own example re-lists every feature it wants active for exactly this reason. Second, a policy with no default block, where every unnamed Region is unmanaged and, because new Regions are only automatically included when a default block is used, no future Region is ever covered. Third, detaching the policy, where the general declarative-policy rule is that the attribute state rolls back to its previous state, but GuardDuty documents an exception: GuardDuty remains enabled in previously covered accounts while future accounts joining or moving into the organizational unit are no longer automatically enabled, so what is lost is future enablement rather than current coverage. A panel contrasts the policy types: service control policies and resource control policies control maximum access permissions at an API level and do not govern service-linked roles, whereas declarative policies enforce the desired configuration of a service without using API actions, are enforced in the service control plane, and do govern service-linked roles. A closing panel notes that policies are managed by the Organizations delegated administrator, that the configuration policy pages are available only to that account, that multiple policies merge into an effective policy with more specific policies closer to the account taking precedence, and that the authored form using the at-at-assign inheritance operator differs from the effective form returned by DescribeEffectivePolicy.
svg.title: Three ways a Region ends up uncovered, and none of them is an error
svg.text: A Region block replaces the default. It does not extend it.
So an override that means “turn one thing off here” turns off everything it forgot to re-list.
The document — at least one block, both optional
guardduty → enablement → {
default: every Region GuardDuty is available in
us-east-1: that Region only, replacing default
8 feature keys · foundational must be enabled in any
block where any other feature is enabled
runtime_monitoring is the only key with sub-features
How a Region resolves
Region block present → it is the whole answer.
“any feature omitted from a Region block is not
inherited from default”
No Region block, default present → the default.
Neither → unmanaged. Not on, not off:
“existing settings are left unchanged”
and unmanaged looks like covered on any policy-driven view
Three ways coverage disappears, none of which errors
1 · The narrow override
default enables foundational,
s3_data_events, ebs_malware.
You add a us-east-1 block with
ebs_malware disabled, alone.
Result: the detector and S3
Protection go too.
2 · No default block
You name the Regions you use.
Every other Region: unmanaged.
“New Regions are automatically
included when using the default
block in a policy.”
No default → no future Region.
3 · Detaching the policy
General rule: the attribute state
“will roll back to its previous state”.
GuardDuty is an exception:
it “remains enabled in previously
covered accounts” — but new
accounts are no longer enabled.
costs nothing today, everything later
Why this needed a new policy type rather than an SCP
SCPs and RCPs — “by controlling the maximum available access permissions” at an API level. Governs service-linked roles: No.
Declarative — “by enforcing the desired configuration of an AWS service without using API actions”. SLRs: Yes.
An SCP can stop someone turning GuardDuty off. Only a declarative policy turns it on.
“enforced in the service’s control plane, which is an important distinction from authorization policies” — so use both, not either.
Reading back what is actually in force
Policies merge: “more specific policies (closer to the account) take precedence”, so the document you wrote is not the answer.
And the two forms differ: authored {“status”:{“@@assign”:“enabled”}} vs effective {“status”:“enabled”}.
A textual diff of authored JSON against DescribeEffectivePolicy reports a change on every single key.
The account status report is the only view that separates “enabled” from “nobody asserted anything here”.
All three failures are the same failure: a configuration that is absent rather than wrong. Absence is what the document cannot show you.
